title: Disagreeing well
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE OPTATIVE IS THE HEDGE, and saying that out loud is the whole module. bhavān gacchet advises without ordering; idam bhinnam syāt supposes without asserting. Neither of them contradicts anybody, and no new cell is opened to do it — the mood was already here.

prāyaḥ is 'probably'. It takes no ending and stands in front of what it softens, exactly where L3-M3's kadācit stands — but kadācit guesses at something and prāyaḥ estimates it, which is why a forecast takes prāyaḥ and a possibility takes kadācit.

prāyaḥ is ONE LETTER from L1-M4's prātaḥ, 'in the morning', and they are two different words that no ending will ever bring together: prāyaḥ ends -yaḥ and prātaḥ ends -taḥ. The hazard is in the writing, not in the grammar.

prāyaḥ is NOT a member of the -taḥ adverb family, exactly as prātaḥ is not. That family is still the nine L2-M4 and L2-M10 left it at — ataḥ, kutaḥ, yataḥ, purataḥ, pṛṣṭhataḥ, vāmataḥ, dakṣiṇataḥ, agrataḥ, tataḥ — and this module adds nobody to it.

bhinnam is 'different', and it is how you disagree without saying anybody is wrong. It is neuter throughout this module, agreeing with idam and with L4-M4's matam, and it claims a difference and nothing more.

saṃśayaḥ is 'a doubt', and it goes into the frame L3-M6 built for a feeling: mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti, 'I have a doubt'. Its ṃ is INSIDE the token — internal sandhi written in full, like L1-M1's saṃskṛtam — and not a word-final nasal, which this course always writes m.
Disagreement still negates the MANNER word and not the verb: L3-M3's na tathā, unchanged. Everything this module adds stands in front of that or behind it, and nothing replaces it.

English hedges with a modal — might, could, I think — so a learner reaches for a WORD where Sanskrit reaches for a MOOD. The commonest error is a flat present with manye bolted on the front, which asserts something and then calls it an opinion.

An English disagreement often opens with an apology. L2-M1's kṣamyatām is an apology for a FAULT, not a softener, so in front of a disagreement it confesses to one. The softeners here are prāyaḥ, kadācit and the optative.

What a face-saving turn still does not get: no prohibition, since mā with the imperative has been refused since L1-M3 and a refusal is still L2-M5's alam; no second-person ending, so a disagreement is addressed to bhavān or bhavatī with a third-person verb; no vocative; and no optative cell beyond L3-M4's three and L4-M3's four.

sentences.display: prāyaḥ idam satyam, kintu mama mate saṃśayaḥ asti.
sentences.script: प्रायः इदम् सत्यम्, किन्तु मम मते संशयः अस्ति।
sentences.cue: This is probably true, but in my opinion there is a doubt.
sentences.literal: probably this true, but my in-opinion doubt is

words.note: 'Probably'. It takes no ending and stands in front of what it softens, like L3-M3's kadācit — but kadācit guesses and prāyaḥ estimates. It is NOT L1-M4's prātaḥ, 'in the morning'.
L1-M1's neuter 'this'. L4-M4 chose it over L3-M2's correlative tat, and a disagreeing module points the same way.
L3-M3's one-word agreement, here softened in front by prāyaḥ. Granting it only probably is what leaves room for the kintu behind.
L1-M10's 'but', at the front of its clause.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
L4-M4's word in its 'in' shape. mama mate is 'in my opinion'; matam is the naming shape of the same word.
'A doubt', masculine, and it sits in L3-M6's frame for a feeling: mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti. The ṃ is INSIDE the word — internal sandhi written in full, like L1-M1's saṃskṛtam.
L1-M3's 'is · there is'. It asserts; syāt supposes, and this module is about the difference.

sentences.trap: prāyaḥ softens the AGREEMENT, not the doubt. Put it in front of the second half instead and you have agreed flatly and then doubted vaguely, which is the opposite arrangement.
sentences.sound: PRAA-yah i-DAM SAT-yam, KIN-tu MA-ma MA-teh sang-SHA-yah AS-ti.

variations.display: idam satyam, kintu mama mate saṃśayaḥ asti.
variations.script: इदम् सत्यम्, किन्तु मम मते संशयः अस्ति।
variations.cue: This is true, but in my opinion there is a doubt.
variations.changed: prāyaḥ is dropped and the first half becomes a flat agreement, so the turn behind it contradicts something you have just asserted yourself

variations.display: prāyaḥ idam na satyam.
variations.script: प्रायः इदम् न सत्यम्।
variations.cue: This is probably not true.
variations.changed: the hedge stays and the claim is negated — prāyaḥ softens a denial exactly as it softens an agreement

variations.display: kim idam satyam? mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti.
variations.script: किम् इदम् सत्यम्? मह्यम् संशयः अस्ति।
variations.cue: Is this true? I have a doubt.
variations.changed: L1-M2's kim turns the claim into a question, which is the softest disagreement this course can make

sentences.usage: The opening move of a polite objection: agree as far as you can, then name the doubt as yours.

sentences.display: na tathā, kintu mama mate idam bhinnam.
sentences.script: न तथा, किन्तु मम मते इदम् भिन्नम्।
sentences.cue: Not so — but in my opinion this is different.
sentences.literal: not so, but my in-opinion this different

words.note: L1-M2's 'not', and here it negates tathā and not a verb. That is L3-M3's second job for this word, unchanged.
L3-M3's 'so', pointing back at what was just said. na tathā disagrees by negating the MANNER word instead of the verb.
L1-M10's 'but', at the front of its clause.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
L4-M4's word in its 'in' shape. mama mate is 'in my opinion'; matam is the naming shape of the same word.
L1-M1's neuter 'this'. L4-M4 chose it over L3-M2's correlative tat, and a disagreeing module points the same way.
'Different', and it is how you disagree without saying anybody is wrong. It is neuter throughout this module, agreeing with idam and with matam.

sentences.trap: na tathā is already the whole disagreement. bhinnam behind it is not a second denial but a softer restatement — you say what it is instead of only what it is not.

variations.display: aham na tathā manye, kintu mama mate idam bhinnam.
variations.script: अहम् न तथा मन्ये, किन्तु मम मते इदम् भिन्नम्।
variations.cue: I do not think so, but in my opinion this is different.
variations.changed: L3-M3's full form with manye: the same disagreement with an owner put on it

variations.display: na tathā, yataḥ mama mate idam bhinnam.
variations.script: न तथा, यतः मम मते इदम् भिन्नम्।
variations.cue: Not so, because in my opinion this is different.
variations.changed: L1-M9's yataḥ turns the second half into the REASON for the disagreement instead of a second claim

variations.display: prāyaḥ na tathā.
variations.script: प्रायः न तथा।
variations.cue: Probably not so.
variations.changed: the hedge goes in front of the disagreement itself, which is as soft as na tathā gets

sentences.usage: Disagreeing and then saying what you actually think. Stopping at na tathā is correct and blunt; this is the same move with somewhere to go.

words.note: L1-M1's neuter 'this'. L4-M4 chose it over L3-M2's correlative tat, and a disagreeing module points the same way.
'Different', and it is how you disagree without saying anybody is wrong. It is neuter throughout this module, agreeing with idam and with matam.
L4-M3's optative of asti, doing its second job. In a counterfactual it was 'would be'; here nothing is supposed away and it is simply 'might be'. Three words and no contradiction in any of them.

sentences.trap: Three words and not one of them says anybody is wrong. This is the mildest disagreement in the course, and the mood is doing all of it.

variations.display: idam bhinnam asti.
variations.script: इदम् भिन्नम् अस्ति।
variations.cue: This is different.
variations.changed: syāt gives way to L1-M3's asti and the supposition becomes an assertion — the same three words now contradict

variations.display: kadācit idam bhinnam.
variations.script: कदाचित् इदम् भिन्नम्।
variations.cue: Perhaps this is different.
variations.changed: L3-M3's kadācit hedges with a word where syāt hedges with a mood; both are open and the sentence needs only one

variations.display: idam bhinnam na syāt.
variations.script: इदम् भिन्नम् न स्यात्।
variations.cue: This might not be different.
variations.changed: the supposition is negated — 'perhaps it is not different after all' — and it is still not a contradiction

mistake.why: Two claims have been stacked with nothing joining them: 'I think' and 'this is different'. L3-M3 settled it — this course has no word for 'that', so the opinion and the claim are two sentences, or the opinion carries tathā: aham tathā manye.

sentences.usage: Said to somebody who has just stated a fact you doubt. It leaves them room to be right.

sentences.display: aham tathā na manye. kadācit idam bhinnam.
sentences.script: अहम् तथा न मन्ये। कदाचित् इदम् भिन्नम्।
sentences.cue: I do not think so. Perhaps this is different.
sentences.literal: I so not think. perhaps this different

words.note: L1-M1's 'I', written once at most.
L3-M3's 'so', pointing back at what was just said. na tathā disagrees by negating the MANNER word instead of the verb.
L1-M2's 'not', in front of the verb it negates.

words.cue: I think · I am of the view
words.note: L3-M3's 'I think', first person only — this course writes no third-person shape of it, so nobody can be asked their opinion with this verb.
L3-M3's softener, in front of what it softens. It hedges with a WORD where the optative hedges with a mood, and this course has both.
L1-M1's neuter 'this'. L4-M4 chose it over L3-M2's correlative tat, and a disagreeing module points the same way.
'Different', and it is how you disagree without saying anybody is wrong. It is neuter throughout this module, agreeing with idam and with matam.

sentences.trap: Two sentences and not one join between them. L3-M3's rule holds: there is no word for 'that' here, so the opinion stops and the claim starts.

variations.display: aham tathā manye. kadācit idam na bhinnam.
variations.script: अहम् तथा मन्ये। कदाचित् इदम् न भिन्नम्।
variations.cue: I think so. Perhaps this is not different.
variations.changed: both halves flip and the shape holds — an opinion, a full stop, and then a hedged claim

variations.display: aham na jānāmi. kadācit idam bhinnam.
variations.script: अहम् न जानामि। कदाचित् इदम् भिन्नम्।
variations.cue: I do not know. Perhaps this is different.
variations.changed: not knowing replaces not agreeing, which is the softer of the two openings and commits you to nothing

variations.display: aham tathā na manye, yataḥ idam bhinnam.
variations.script: अहम् तथा न मन्ये, यतः इदम् भिन्नम्।
variations.cue: I do not think so, because this is different.
variations.changed: the two sentences become one with L1-M9's yataḥ, which supplies the join English would make with 'because'

sentences.usage: The everyday disagreement. The hedge is in the second sentence, so the first one can be as plain as you like.

sentences.display: prāyaḥ bhavān gacchet, kintu mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti.
sentences.script: प्रायः भवान् गच्छेत्, किन्तु मह्यम् संशयः अस्ति।
sentences.cue: You should probably go, but I have a doubt.
sentences.literal: probably you should-go, but to-me doubt is

words.note: 'Probably'. It takes no ending and stands in front of what it softens, like L3-M3's kadācit — but kadācit guesses and prāyaḥ estimates. It is NOT L1-M4's prātaḥ, 'in the morning'.
L1-M2's polite 'you', with a third-person verb. A disagreement is addressed here and nowhere else — this course writes no second-person ending at all.
L3-M4's optative. It advises rather than orders, and prāyaḥ in front of it stops even the advice from sounding settled.
L1-M10's 'but', at the front of its clause.
L1-M1's aham in its 'to me' shape, in L3-M6's frame for what somebody feels.
'A doubt', masculine, and it sits in L3-M6's frame for a feeling: mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti. The ṃ is INSIDE the word — internal sandhi written in full, like L1-M1's saṃskṛtam.
L1-M3's 'is · there is'. It asserts; syāt supposes, and this module is about the difference.

sentences.trap: Two hedges, one sentence, and they are different in kind: prāyaḥ hedges the word, the optative hedges the verb. Neither cancels the other.
sentences.sound: PRAA-yah bha-VAAN GACH-chet, KIN-tu MAH-yam sang-SHA-yah AS-ti.

variations.display: bhavān gacchet, kintu mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti.
variations.script: भवान् गच्छेत्, किन्तु मह्यम् संशयः अस्ति।
variations.cue: You should go, but I have a doubt.
variations.changed: prāyaḥ is dropped and the advice hardens — the optative alone still advises, but it no longer sounds unsettled

variations.display: prāyaḥ bhavān na gacchet, yataḥ mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti.
variations.script: प्रायः भवान् न गच्छेत्, यतः मह्यम् संशयः अस्ति।
variations.cue: You should probably not go, because I have a doubt.
variations.changed: the advice is negated and the doubt becomes its reason, with L1-M9's yataḥ marking the link

variations.display: kim bhavān gacchet? mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti.
variations.script: किम् भवान् गच्छेत्? मह्यम् संशयः अस्ति।
variations.cue: Should you go? I have a doubt.
variations.changed: the advice becomes a question and the doubt is left standing behind it, owned but not pressed

mistake.display: prāyaḥ bhavān gacchatu, kintu mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti.
mistake.why: gacchatu is L2-M4's polite imperative and it ORDERS, however courteously. prāyaḥ in front of an order contradicts it — nobody can probably-command. The hedge needs the optative gacchet behind it.

sentences.usage: How to advise something you are not sure of. Owning the doubt with mahyam is what keeps it from sounding like a warning.

sentences.display: prāyaḥ bhavataḥ matam uttamam, tathāpi mama matam bhinnam.
sentences.script: प्रायः भवतः मतम् उत्तमम्, तथापि मम मतम् भिन्नम्।
sentences.cue: Your opinion is probably excellent; even so my view is different.
sentences.literal: probably of-you opinion excellent, even-so my opinion different

words.note: 'Probably'. It takes no ending and stands in front of what it softens, like L3-M3's kadācit — but kadācit guesses and prāyaḥ estimates. It is NOT L1-M4's prātaḥ, 'in the morning'.
L1-M2's bhavān in its 'of you' shape, to a man; bhavatyāḥ to a woman.
L4-M4's word in its naming shape, here the subject of the first clause. The second clause uses the same shape for mine.
L2-M3's praise, agreeing with the neuter matam. Praising the view before differing from it is L4-M4's order, reused.
L1-M10's 'even so', at the front of the clause it turns.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
The same word again, now mine. Two opinions named side by side is what makes this a difference rather than a correction.
'Different', and it is how you disagree without saying anybody is wrong. It is neuter throughout this module, agreeing with idam and with matam.

sentences.trap: Nobody is wrong in this sentence. bhinnam says the two views differ and stops there, which is the only thing this module ever claims.

variations.display: prāyaḥ bhavatyāḥ matam uttamam, tathāpi mama matam bhinnam.
variations.script: प्रायः भवत्याः मतम् उत्तमम्, तथापि मम मतम् भिन्नम्।
variations.cue: Your opinion is probably excellent; even so my view is different.
variations.changed: the listener is a woman, so bhavataḥ becomes bhavatyāḥ and nothing else in the sentence knows

variations.display: avaśyam bhavataḥ matam uttamam, tathāpi mama matam bhinnam.
variations.script: अवश्यम् भवतः मतम् उत्तमम्, तथापि मम मतम् भिन्नम्।
variations.cue: Certainly your opinion is excellent; even so my view is different.
variations.changed: L4-M4's avaśyam grants the point outright where prāyaḥ only estimates it — a stronger concession in front of the same turn

variations.display: prāyaḥ bhavataḥ matam uttamam, kintu mama matam bhinnam syāt.
variations.script: प्रायः भवतः मतम् उत्तमम्, किन्तु मम मतम् भिन्नम् स्यात्।
variations.cue: Your opinion is probably excellent, but my view might be different.
variations.changed: syāt enters the second half and the difference becomes something supposed rather than declared

sentences.usage: The sentence for a meeting. Two views are named, neither is scored, and the disagreement survives to the next turn.

sentences.cue: Perhaps my view might be different.

words.note: L3-M3's softener, in front of what it softens. It hedges with a WORD where the optative hedges with a mood, and this course has both.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
L4-M4's word in its naming shape — here the opinion itself is what the sentence is about. The 'in' shape is mate.
'Different', and it is how you disagree without saying anybody is wrong. It is neuter throughout this module, agreeing with idam and with matam.
L4-M3's optative of asti. With kadācit already in front, the sentence hedges twice, which in this register is ordinary rather than excessive.

sentences.trap: kadācit and syāt hedge the same claim in two different ways, and a speaker really does use both. One would be enough; two is politeness rather than error.

variations.display: mama matam bhinnam syāt.
variations.script: मम मतम् भिन्नम् स्यात्।
variations.cue: My view might be different.
variations.changed: kadācit is dropped and the optative carries the whole hedge alone, which is this module's lesson in four words

variations.display: kadācit bhavataḥ matam bhinnam syāt.
variations.script: कदाचित् भवतः मतम् भिन्नम् स्यात्।
variations.cue: Perhaps your view might be different.
variations.changed: the differing view becomes the listener's; nothing about the mood moves when the owner does

variations.display: kadācit mama matam bhinnam na syāt.
variations.script: कदाचित् मम मतम् भिन्नम् न स्यात्।
variations.cue: Perhaps my view is not different after all.
variations.changed: the supposition is negated, which is how a disagreement is quietly withdrawn

sentences.usage: Said when you want it on record that you differ and off the record who is right.

sentences.display: prāyaḥ adya vṛṣṭiḥ syāt, ataḥ bhavān na gacchet.
sentences.script: प्रायः अद्य वृष्टिः स्यात्, अतः भवान् न गच्छेत्।
sentences.cue: It will probably rain today, so you should not go.
sentences.literal: probably today rain might-be, so you not should-go

words.note: 'Probably'. It takes no ending and stands in front of what it softens, like L3-M3's kadācit — but kadācit guesses and prāyaḥ estimates. It is NOT L1-M4's prātaḥ, 'in the morning'.
L1-M4's 'today'. A forecast needs its day said, because no verb here carries a tense.
L4-M2's rain in its naming shape, as the subject of syāt. L4-M2's own sentences use the ablative vṛṣṭeḥ, which would mean 'because of the rain' and is a different job.
L4-M3's optative of asti, and the whole of a forecast. asti would REPORT the rain; syāt supposes it, which is the difference between looking out of the window and guessing.
L1-M9's 'so', heading the consequence. L4-M2 settled the placement: one link takes this marker or yataḥ, never both.
L1-M2's polite 'you', with a third-person verb. A disagreement is addressed here and nowhere else — this course writes no second-person ending at all.
L1-M2's 'not', in front of the verb it negates.
L3-M4's optative, advising. Both verbs in this sentence are optatives and neither of them is a counterfactual — L4-M3's frame is absent and so is its meaning.

sentences.trap: A forecast is a hedge about the world and advice is a hedge about a person, and Sanskrit spends the same mood on both. Two optatives here, one counterfactual nowhere.
sentences.sound: PRAA-yah A-dya VRISH-tih SYAAT, a-TAH bha-VAAN NA GACH-chet.

variations.display: adya vṛṣṭiḥ asti, ataḥ bhavān na gacchet.
variations.script: अद्य वृष्टिः अस्ति, अतः भवान् न गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: It is raining today, so you should not go.
variations.changed: the rain is asserted instead of supposed, and the advice behind it stops being a guess

variations.display: prāyaḥ adya vṛṣṭiḥ syāt, tathāpi aham gacchāmi.
variations.script: प्रायः अद्य वृष्टिः स्यात्, तथापि अहम् गच्छामि।
variations.cue: It will probably rain today; even so I am going.
variations.changed: ataḥ gives way to L1-M10's tathāpi and the same forecast becomes a reason to go anyway

variations.display: prāyaḥ adya vṛṣṭiḥ na syāt.
variations.script: प्रायः अद्य वृष्टिः न स्यात्।
variations.cue: It probably will not rain today.
variations.changed: the forecast is negated and the advice dropped — a hedged prediction stands perfectly well on its own

mistake.display: prāyaḥ adya vṛṣṭiḥ, ataḥ bhavān na gacchet.
mistake.why: The first clause has been left verbless, so it asserts: 'there IS rain today'. prāyaḥ softens how sure you are, but the sentence still reports. syāt is what turns a report into a forecast.

sentences.usage: Weather and advice in one breath, which is most of what hedging is for.

sentences.display: aham na jānāmi, mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti.
sentences.script: अहम् न जानामि, मह्यम् संशयः अस्ति।
sentences.cue: I do not know — I have a doubt.
sentences.literal: I not know, to-me doubt is

words.note: L1-M1's 'I', written once at most.
L1-M2's 'not', in front of the verb it negates.
L2-M8's 'I know'. Negated it is the most honest disagreement there is, because it claims nothing at all.
L1-M1's aham in its 'to me' shape, in L3-M6's frame for what somebody feels.
'A doubt', masculine, and it sits in L3-M6's frame for a feeling: mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti. The ṃ is INSIDE the word — internal sandhi written in full, like L1-M1's saṃskṛtam.
L1-M3's 'is · there is'. It asserts; syāt supposes, and this module is about the difference.

sentences.trap: Not knowing is not the same as disagreeing, and this course keeps them apart: na jānāmi says nothing about who is right, while na tathā does.

variations.display: aham jānāmi, kintu mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti.
variations.script: अहम् जानामि, किन्तु मह्यम् संशयः अस्ति।
variations.cue: I know, but I have a doubt.
variations.changed: knowing and doubting stand in one sentence, joined by L1-M10's kintu — a different admission and a more useful one

variations.display: mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti, ataḥ aham na jānāmi.
variations.script: मह्यम् संशयः अस्ति, अतः अहम् न जानामि।
variations.cue: I have a doubt, so I do not know.
variations.changed: L1-M9's ataḥ marks the link at the other end and the doubt becomes the reason for the not-knowing

variations.display: aham na jānāmi. prāyaḥ bhavān jānāti.
variations.script: अहम् न जानामि। प्रायः भवान् जानाति।
variations.cue: I do not know. You probably know.
variations.changed: the second sentence hands the question back, hedged; jānāti is the same verb in the shape bhavān takes

sentences.usage: The safest thing to say when you disagree and cannot say why yet.

sentences.display: mama mate idam na uttamam, kintu aham na kruddhaḥ.
sentences.script: मम मते इदम् न उत्तमम्, किन्तु अहम् न क्रुद्धः।
sentences.cue: In my opinion this is not good, but I am not angry.
sentences.literal: my in-opinion this not excellent, but I not angry

words.note: L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
L4-M4's word in its 'in' shape. mama mate is 'in my opinion'; matam is the naming shape of the same word.
L1-M1's neuter 'this'. L4-M4 chose it over L3-M2's correlative tat, and a disagreeing module points the same way.
L1-M2's 'not', in front of the verb it negates.
L2-M3's praise, negated. na uttamam is a judgement about the thing and about nobody in the room.
L1-M10's 'but', at the front of its clause.
L1-M1's 'I', written once at most.
L1-M2's 'not' a second time, now in front of an adjective standing as a whole clause. There is no verb here for it to reach.
L3-M6's 'angry', forking with the speaker: kruddhā from a woman. Saying you are not is how a disagreement stops being a quarrel.

sentences.trap: The second half is what saves the face, and it is not politeness for its own sake: without it a flat na uttamam in this register reads as displeasure rather than as a view.
sentences.sound: MA-ma MA-teh i-DAM NA UT-ta-mam, KIN-tu a-HAM NA KRUD-dhah.

variations.display: mama mate idam na uttamam, tathāpi aham santuṣṭaḥ.
variations.script: मम मते इदम् न उत्तमम्, तथापि अहम् सन्तुष्टः।
variations.cue: In my opinion this is not good; even so I am content.
variations.changed: the second half turns positive with L1-M10's tathāpi — disagreeing and being content are not in conflict

variations.display: prāyaḥ idam na uttamam, kintu aham na kruddhaḥ.
variations.script: प्रायः इदम् न उत्तमम्, किन्तु अहम् न क्रुद्धः।
variations.cue: This is probably not good, but I am not angry.
variations.changed: mama mate gives way to prāyaḥ, so the judgement is hedged rather than owned, and it names nobody

variations.display: mama mate idam na uttamam. kim bhavataḥ matam bhinnam?
variations.script: मम मते इदम् न उत्तमम्। किम् भवतः मतम् भिन्नम्?
variations.cue: In my opinion this is not good. Is your view different?
variations.changed: the second half hands the floor back as a question, which is how a disagreement stays a conversation

mistake.display: kṣamyatām, mama mate idam na uttamam.
mistake.why: kṣamyatām is L2-M1's apology for a FAULT. In front of a disagreement it says you have done something wrong and are sorry for it, which is not what you meant at all. A disagreement is softened by prāyaḥ, by kadācit or by the optative, and never by an apology.

sentences.usage: How to leave a disagreement without leaving a grudge. In this register the second clause does more work than the first.
sentences.mnemonic: Differ about the thing, not about the person.

comprehensionPool.display: prāyaḥ idam uttamam, kintu mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti.
comprehensionPool.script: प्रायः इदम् उत्तमम्, किन्तु मह्यम् संशयः अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: This is probably excellent, but I have a doubt.
In my opinion this is different.
Not so — the road is probably long.

comprehensionPool.display: aham na jānāmi, kintu idam bhinnam syāt.
comprehensionPool.script: अहम् न जानामि, किन्तु इदम् भिन्नम् स्यात्।
comprehensionPool.cue: I do not know, but this might be different.
He is probably not going today.

comprehensionPool.display: mahyam saṃśayaḥ asti, ataḥ aham na tathā manye.
comprehensionPool.script: मह्यम् संशयः अस्ति, अतः अहम् न तथा मन्ये।
comprehensionPool.cue: I have a doubt, so I do not think so.

comprehensionPool.display: prāyaḥ mama matam na uttamam, tathāpi aham tathā manye.
comprehensionPool.script: प्रायः मम मतम् न उत्तमम्, तथापि अहम् तथा मन्ये।
comprehensionPool.cue: My view is probably not good; even so I think so.

comprehensionPool.display: idam kāryam bhinnam syāt, kintu hitam.
comprehensionPool.script: इदम् कार्यम् भिन्नम् स्यात्, किन्तु हितम्।
comprehensionPool.cue: This work might be different, but it is good for us.
Perhaps this is not different after all.

comprehensionPool.display: prāyaḥ adya vṛṣṭiḥ syāt, ataḥ mārgaḥ na uttamaḥ.
comprehensionPool.script: प्रायः अद्य वृष्टिः स्यात्, अतः मार्गः न उत्तमः।
comprehensionPool.cue: It will probably rain today, so the road will not be good.

comprehensionPool.display: bhavataḥ matam śrutvā mama saṃśayaḥ na asti.
comprehensionPool.script: भवतः मतम् श्रुत्वा मम संशयः न अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: Having heard your opinion I have no doubt.

comprehensionPool.display: prāyaḥ bhavatī jānāti, kintu aham na jānāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: प्रायः भवती जानाति, किन्तु अहम् न जानामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: You probably know, but I do not.
